AI4MOBILITY · DIFFUSION IN TRANSPORTATION

Thirty-five transportation papers that use diffusion, and how each one uses it

Each card shows a paper’s model architecture figure and answers the same six questions about its diffusion model. Read them as variations on one recipe. Diffusion is a training method, not a network: the same noise-and-denoise recipe trains a transformer over vehicles and time steps, a U-Net over camera images, or a small network over detector speeds. What changes from paper to paper is what gets noised, what the network reads, and how sampling is steered.

The papers

Filter by transportation problem, by the network that denoises, by where the denoising happens, or by how sampling is steered. Or jump to a year.

1 · Safety-critical driving scenarios

Start from a model of normal traffic and steer its sampling toward the conflicts a planner must survive.

CTG

Zhong et al. · ICRA 2023 · paper · [D01]
Safety-critical driving scenariosU-NetRaw data
1What is noised (x)
Each vehicle's future action sequence: acceleration and yaw rate at each step (horizon length not stated). Positions, speed and heading are always computed from the actions with a unicycle vehicle model.
2Condition (c)
An agent-centered raster map plus the past states of the vehicle and its neighbors. A ResNet encodes this; the feature is joined with the step k and added to the convolution features in every U-Net block.
3Denoiser network
A U-Net-like stack of 1-D temporal convolution blocks running along the trajectory (following Diffuser). It reads the noisy actions and the states rolled out from them. Parameter count not stated.
4Training
Graded against the clean trajectory: the network outputs clean actions, states are rolled out, and squared error is taken on both. K = 100 noise steps with a cosine schedule. Trained on nuScenes.
5Sampling
Starts from pure Gaussian noise and takes K = 100 DDPM-style steps; states are re-rolled from actions at every step. In simulation each vehicle re-plans at 2 Hz and executes the first few actions. Runtime not stated.
6Steering
Cost guidance: at each step the predicted mean takes a few clipped Adam gradient steps on an STL rule's robustness score. Several guided samples are drawn and the best is kept (filtration). Collision rules guide all vehicles jointly.

How diffusion works here. CTG learns how nuScenes drivers choose acceleration and turn rate over the next few seconds, given a local map image and nearby vehicles' recent motion. Training noises these action sequences and asks a 1-D convolutional U-Net to recover the clean sequence; positions come from rolling the actions through a simple vehicle (unicycle) model, so every sample is drivable. Sampling starts from noise and runs 100 denoising steps. At each step, a traffic rule written in signal temporal logic (STL, a formal language for rules over time, such as 'always below the speed limit') gives a score whose gradient nudges the plan. Idea worth remembering: train once on ordinary driving, then add new rules only at sampling time.

Used for: Realistic, rule-following background traffic for closed-loop AV simulation of nuScenes scenes: speed limits, target speeds, goal waypoints, stop signs, no collisions, no off-road driving.

What they found
  • Speed-limit rule (Table II): plain samples from the trained model, with no guidance or filtration (row 'CTG (w/o f+g)'), had a rule violation of 1.380, realism deviation 0.396 and failure rate 0.301.
  • With STL guidance and best-of-several filtration (row 'CTG', Table II), the same model cut the violation to 0.019, and realism deviation (0.359) and failure rate (0.165) also improved; lower is better for all three.

For mobility: A simulation team could write local rules (speed limits, stop signs, target speeds) as formulas and get realistic, rule-following background traffic without retraining the model.

Watch out: Rules and realism pull against each other: more guidance steps cut violations but worsen realism and failure rate, and only vehicles were modeled, not pedestrians or cyclists.

CTG++

Zhong et al. · CoRL 2023 · paper · [D02]
Safety-critical driving scenariosTransformerRaw data
1What is noised (x)
Future action sequences (acceleration, yaw rate) for all vehicles in a nuScenes scene at once, at 0.1 s steps (horizon length not stated). States come from a unicycle model.
2Condition (c)
Each vehicle's past states, joined to the noisy future along the time axis; its agent-centered vector map, read by map attention; and pairwise relative positions, headings and speeds, read by spatial attention. Step k enters as a sinusoidal code.
3Denoiser network
A spatial-temporal transformer: attention along each vehicle's timeline, then attention between vehicles at each timestep, then attention to the map; this block repeats L times. Parameter count not stated.
4Training
Graded against the clean action trajectory, with rolled-out states also supervised (squared error). K = 100, cosine schedule. 50K iterations, about 10 hours on one RTX 3090, Adam, learning rate 1e-4.
5Sampling
Starts from Gaussian noise and runs K = 100 DDPM-style steps, as in CTG. Closed-loop simulations last 10 s with re-planning at 2 Hz; each scenario takes about 1 minute.
6Steering
LLM-written cost: GPT-4, shown helper functions and example request-to-code pairs, turns a sentence into a differentiable Python loss. Its gradient shifts the predicted mean with clipped Adam steps at every step; the best of several samples is kept.
Denoises inRaw data
NetworkTransformer
Graded onclean data
Steeringconditioning
LLM-written cost
cost guidance
best of many

How diffusion works here. CTG++ fixes two gaps in CTG. CTG planned each vehicle alone, so a follower might ignore a braking leader. CTG++ denoises all vehicles' action sequences together with a transformer that attends across time, across vehicles and to the map. Training matches CTG: noise the actions and grade the network's clean prediction. Second, writing rule formulas needs expertise, so the user types a request instead. GPT-4, shown helper functions and example request-to-code pairs, writes a loss function in Python. During sampling, that loss's gradient nudges every denoising step. Idea worth remembering: the LLM never draws trajectories; it only writes the cost, and the diffusion model keeps the motion realistic.

Used for: Building AV test scenes from plain-English requests, such as 'vehicle A should collide with vehicle B', with realistic, interacting background traffic.

What they found
  • Across eight rule settings on nuScenes (Table 1), CTG++ had the lowest failure rate and scene-level realism deviation in 7 out of 8, against CTG, BITS and BITS+opt.
  • For the GPT-written 'keep distance' request (Table 1), CTG and CTG++ both met it (violation 0.000), but the failure rate (vehicles crashing or leaving the road) was 0.173 for CTG++ vs 0.343 for CTG.

For mobility: An agency could turn written crash-report narratives into simulated test scenes, letting an LLM write the cost while a trained traffic model supplies realistic motion.

Watch out: GPT-4's loss code is not checked automatically and can encode the wrong meaning, map-heavy requests are unsupported, and switching to scene-centered coordinates made failures far more common.

SAFE-SIM

Chang et al. · ECCV 2024 · paper · [D03]
Safety-critical driving scenariosU-NetRaw data
1What is noised (x)
Each non-AV vehicle's next 3.2 s of actions (acceleration, yaw rate) at 0.1 s steps, rolled into positions with a unicycle model. One chosen vehicle plays the adversary.
2Condition (c)
An agent-centered raster map and about 1 s of past states of nearby vehicles, encoded by a ResNet, following CTG's architecture. The paper gives no further detail on how it enters the denoiser.
3Denoiser network
A UNet-like stack of 1-D temporal convolution blocks over the trajectory, as in CTG. Parameter count not stated.
4Training
Graded against the clean trajectory (squared error). K = 100, cosine schedule with β from 0.0001 to 0.05. 70,000 iterations on four RTX A6000 GPUs, Adam, learning rate 1e-5, nuScenes train split.
5Sampling
Starts from pure noise, or (partial diffusion) from a rule-made crash proposal noised to step γ·K. Draws 20 samples per vehicle and keeps one. Re-plans at 2 Hz; Table 2 lists 104.5 ± 17.7 s simulation time on nuScenes.
6Steering
Cost guidance on the predicted clean plan each step: approach the AV at a set relative speed and time to collision, stay on route, keep apart. A noised crash sketch sets crash type; the adversary keeps its most adversarial sample.

NetworkU-Net
Graded onclean data
Steeringconditioning
cost guidance

best of many

How diffusion works here. SAFE-SIM replays a real nuScenes scene, but a diffusion model drives the other cars and re-plans twice a second as the AV moves. The model, built like CTG, learns to recover clean 3.2-second action plans from noised ones. While sampling, one chosen car's plan is nudged at each step by cost gradients: get close to the AV at a chosen relative speed or time to collision. Other costs keep every car on its route and apart. To pick a front, side or rear crash, a rule-made sketch of it is partly noised and then denoised, so it keeps its shape but becomes drivable. Idea worth remembering: one trained model gives many tests, changed only by costs and starting sketches.

Used for: Closed-loop safety testing of AV planners (rule-based, IDM, behavior cloning, BITS, PDM-Closed) against reactive adversaries whose crash type and aggressiveness can be set.

What they found
  • On nuScenes with a rule-based AV planner (Table 2), the SAFE-SIM adversary caused a collision in 43.2% of scenes vs 36.4% for STRIVE, with better realism (0.38 vs 0.85; lower is better).
  • Partial diffusion, starting from noised rule-made crash sketches, raised the collision rate from 23.9% to 29.0% and the variance of collision points from 1.62 m to 5.44 m, i.e. more varied crashes (Table 5).

For mobility: A safety team could turn recorded real scenes into many reactive crash tests, choosing crash type and severity, to stress an automated vehicle's planner before road testing.

Watch out: Realism is judged only by acceleration and jerk histograms; some adversaries hit other cars before the AV, and some crashes are not the AV's fault.

AdvDiffuser

Xie et al. · arXiv 2024 · paper · [D05]
Safety-critical driving scenariosU-NetAutoencoder latent
1What is noised (x)
A latent code for each background vehicle, made by a VAE-style posterior network from its future path; a decoder turns codes into 6 s trajectories. Latent size not stated.
2Condition (c)
A context encoder reads history and map: an MLP state embedding h and a two-layer graph network giving a prior code z per vehicle. z is concatenated with the noisy latent; h enters through adaptive group normalization.
3Denoiser network
A U-Net that predicts the added noise. Its clean latent is decoded by an autoregressive trajectory decoder (graph interaction net, RNN memory, bicycle model). Parameter count not stated.
4Training
Graded against the noise (L2 loss), with clean latents from the posterior network. Modules trained separately, then jointly with an ELBO loss plus a collision penalty. 200 epochs, Adam, learning rate 5×10⁻⁴, batch 8. K and schedule not stated.
5Sampling
Starts from a random latent and runs K reverse steps with an update written following DDIM; the decoder then produces trajectories. K not stated. Table II marks it as real-time (above 10 Hz).
6Steering
Learned-reward guidance: a DQN-style network scores how much a latent leads to the AV crashing, minus penalties for other crashes. Its gradient shifts the predicted mean each step. A short online warm-up adapts it to a new planner.
Denoises inAutoencoder latent
NetworkU-Net
Graded onnoise
Steeringconditioning
learned-reward guidance

How diffusion works here. AdvDiffuser first compresses each background vehicle's future path into a short latent code with a VAE-style encoder, and learns a decoder that turns codes back into drivable paths through a bicycle model. A U-Net is trained to predict the noise added to these codes, given map, history and interaction features. A separate small reward network learns, by reinforcement learning, how likely a code leads to the AV crashing while other cars stay safe. At sampling time, codes start as noise; each denoising step is nudged by the reward's gradient, then the result is decoded. Idea worth remembering: realism lives in the diffusion model and aggression in a small reward model, so only that part is retuned per planner.

Used for: Generating adversarial background traffic from nuScenes logs to test AV planners (rule-based, SimNet, TrafficSim), and adapting the attack to a new planner after a short warm-up.

What they found
  • Latent vs raw diffusion (Table I): running diffusion directly on trajectories ('traj2traj') gave minSFDE of 931 m and velocity JSD of 21.27 (in hundredths), versus 2.21 m and 0.81 for diffusion in the latent space.
  • Against a rule-based planner (Table II), guided AdvDiffuser made the AV crash in 11.03% of scenarios while only 0.27% of background vehicles hit each other; only AdvSim, which is not real-time, caused more AV crashes.

For mobility: A test team could keep one realistic traffic generator and retrain only a small reward model to probe each new driving stack, instead of rebuilding adversaries from scratch.

Watch out: AV crash rates stay modest, the paper omits diffusion steps and noise schedule, and the authors themselves question how relevant such adversarial scenes are to real-world safety.

DiffScene

Xu, Petiushko, Zhao & Li · AAAI 2025 · paper · [D04]
Safety-critical driving scenariosNot statedRaw data
1What is noised (x)
The adversarial surrounding vehicle's whole trajectory: a matrix of states and actions at each timestep up to the horizon T. Sizes not stated.
2Condition (c)
None stated: the denoiser reads only the noisy trajectory and step k. After each step, the trajectory's first state is reset to the real starting state.
3Denoiser network
Not stated in the paper.
4Training
Graded against the clean trajectory (squared error). Cosine schedule; K not stated. Data: 6,995 ordinary CARLA trajectories from trained RL drivers. A separate network learns to predict the objective from 4,000 generated trajectories per setting.
5Sampling
Starts from Gaussian noise and makes one reverse pass for the whole trajectory, with no re-planning; the authors say this allows real-time generation. Number of steps, sampler and runtime not stated.
6Steering
Learned-objective guidance: after each denoising step, N gradient steps (0 to 30 tested) on a weighted mix of safety (close to or hitting the AV), functionality (blocking its route) and constraint (typical speed), as predicted by the learned network.
Denoises inRaw data
NetworkNot stated
Graded onclean data
Steeringlearned-reward guidance
fill-in (inpainting / fixed values)

How diffusion works here. DiffScene first trains a diffusion model on 6,995 ordinary trajectories collected in the CARLA simulator from trained RL drivers, so it learns what normal driving looks like. The model learns to recover a clean state-and-action trajectory from a noised one. To make a test, sampling starts from noise. After every denoising step, a few gradient steps push the trajectory toward danger: get close to or hit the AV, stop it finishing its route, keep a typical speed. Collisions need a simulator run, so a small network is trained to predict these scores and supply gradients. The trajectory's start is then reset to the true start state. Idea worth remembering: the number of push steps trades danger against naturalness.

Used for: Generating safety-critical CARLA test scenarios from three NHTSA pre-crash types to test, and then retrain, RL-based AV driving agents.

What they found
  • Crossing-negotiation setting (S1), averaged over three RL driving agents (Table 1): DiffScene scenarios gave a collision rate of 0.85 ± 0.08 vs 0.72 ± 0.11 for STRIVE (ST), the best baseline, and 0.19 ± 0.03 for adversarial RL.
  • After fine-tuning a SAC driving agent on S1 scenarios (Table 3), its collision rate was 0.26 with DiffScene scenarios vs 0.32 with the best baseline (LC) and 0.90 before fine-tuning.

For mobility: A safety team could take a crash typology such as NHTSA's pre-crash scenarios and generate many realistic, risky variants to test and retrain driving software.

Watch out: All results are in CARLA against RL drivers, not real traffic logs; the main paper does not describe the denoiser network; more push steps add danger but cost naturalness.

CCDiff

Lin et al. · CVPR 2025 · paper · [D07]
Safety-critical driving scenariosTransformerRaw data
1What is noised (x)
The joint state–action trajectories of all agents: future actions over 52 steps at 0.1 s (Table 8), turned into positions by vehicle dynamics. The plan is redone in closed loop, every 0.5 s in the main tests.
2Condition (c)
Each agent's 3-s history, a rasterized map (ResNet-18 features fed to the decoder), and a decision causal graph (time-to-collision mask × attention) that limits which other agents each agent may attend to.
3Denoiser network
A transformer: a temporal tokenizer per agent, spatial cross-attention between agents masked by the causal graph, and an action decoder (2 decoder layers, 16 heads). 15.4M parameters in total, including the CNN map encoder.
4Training
Classical DDPM with 100 denoising steps; the output is graded against the clean actions a(0). The causal graph is randomly swapped for a diagonal one (no interactions) so classifier-free guidance works later. Schedule type not stated.
5Sampling
Starts from pure noise and runs 100 DDPM reverse steps (Table 8); after each step the actions pass through vehicle dynamics. About 20 ms per frame per agent on a V100 GPU.
6Steering
Classifier-free guidance blends the 'no-interaction' and 'causal-parents' predictions (weight w in [1, 2)). Then collision and off-road cost gradients are applied only to the top-ranked key agents; the others are left unguided.
Denoises inRaw data
NetworkTransformer
Graded onclean data
Steeringclassifier-free guidance
cost guidance

How diffusion works here. CCDiff generates the next few seconds of actions for every vehicle in a nuScenes scene and re-plans in closed loop. A transformer denoiser reads each vehicle's history, the map, and a causal graph that says which vehicles influence which. The graph comes from time-to-collision checks and attention weights. Training is standard DDPM, with the graph sometimes removed so the model also learns a 'no-interaction' version. When sampling, classifier-free guidance mixes the two versions, and collision cost gradients push only the top-ranked key agents. Idea worth remembering: steer only the few vehicles that matter, and the rest of the traffic stays realistic.

Used for: Closed-loop generation of safety-critical scenarios (cut-ins, left-turn conflicts, chain-reaction crashes) on nuScenes to test automated-vehicle planners.

What they found
  • With an added over-speed guidance cost, CCDiff's off-road rate was 0.89 vs 4.23 for CTG, and its comfort distance 9.65 vs 15.81 (lower is better for both), at a similar over-speed rate (Table 7).
  • Guiding only the key agents cut the share of agents whose realism and guidance gradients point in conflicting directions from ∼9.1% (CTG) to ∼4.8% (Table 7, Appendix C.1).

For mobility: A safety team could build near-miss tests where only the interacting vehicles are pushed toward conflict, while background traffic keeps behaving like real traffic.

Watch out: The causal graph rests on tuned thresholds (time-to-collision 3.0 s, number of key agents), and the authors note the causal reasoning is hard to evaluate directly.

LangTraj

Chang et al. · ICCV 2025 · paper · [D08]
Safety-critical driving scenariosTransformerRaw data
1What is noised (x)
The joint future action trajectories of all agents in a Waymo scene, 8.0 s ahead at 0.5-s steps, turned into positions by simple unicycle dynamics.
2Condition (c)
Map and 1.1-s agent histories through a query-centric scene encoder (agent–context cross-attention), and a sentence embedded by DistilBERT, fine-tuned with LoRA (a light add-on), fused with each agent's context (text cross-attention).
3Denoiser network
Stacked transformer blocks with three attention types: across agents' future trajectories, from each agent to its scene context, and from each agent to its language embedding. Parameter count not stated.
4Training
Output graded against the clean trajectory; cosine schedule, K = 100; text and history dropped 50% of the time. Then distilled to K = 5 and fine-tuned in closed loop on its own executed samples (best of 8).
5Sampling
DDIM sampler, K = 5 steps from pure noise. 64 joint samples are drawn and the one with the lowest collision loss is kept. About 4.66 s per 8-s simulation with 1 Hz replanning on one A6000 GPU.
6Steering
Classifier-free guidance on the sentence (moderate weights keep realism). For crash tests, guidance on the clean estimate with a collision cost pulls a chosen adversary toward its target agent. Best-of-64 selection by collision loss.
Denoises inRaw data
NetworkTransformer

classifier-free guidance

How diffusion works here. LangTraj generates the joint future motion of all agents in a Waymo scene from noise. It is conditioned on the map, recent history and a sentence such as 'A1 yields to A2'. A transformer denoiser attends across agents, to the scene context and to the sentence. Language is built in during training, using the human-labeled InterDrive interactions; text is dropped half the time so classifier-free guidance works. The model is then cut to 5 denoising steps and fine-tuned in closed loop to recover from its own drift. For crash tests, a collision cost pulls one agent toward another. Idea worth remembering: teach behaviors through words in training instead of hand-writing a cost for each one.

Used for: Language-controlled multi-agent traffic simulation on Waymo data, including text-specified safety-critical scenarios for automated-vehicle testing.

What they found
  • Conditioning on InterDrive's language labels cut trajectory error (minADE, the error of the best sample) by 13.6% versus the same model without text, with realism unchanged (Sec. 6.2–6.3, Table 4).
  • In text-conditioned crash generation with collision guidance, LangTraj reached a 10% higher collision rate than LLM-written guidance functions in the CTG++ style (Sec. 6.5, Table 5).

For mobility: A test engineer could describe interactions in plain words ('A2 merges in front of A1') to build interaction test suites without coding behavior rules.

Watch out: When the sentence conflicts with the last second of motion, the model tends to follow the history, and minADE may not fully show whether the instruction was obeyed.

Safety validation (Wang et al.)

Wang, Schlichting, Delecki & Kochenderfer · arXiv 2025 · paper · [D09]
Safety-critical driving scenariosU-NetRaw data
1What is noised (x)
Not trajectories: a sequence of the ego vehicle's sensor errors on the intruder's relative position and speed (εx, εy, εvx, εvy) over 23 time steps.
2Condition (c)
The denoising step k, the starting relative position and speed of the two vehicles s0, and a robustness threshold (wanted minimum gap; 0 means a crash). How these enter the U-Net is not stated.
3Denoiser network
A U-Net with four downsampling and four upsampling layers, built in PyTorch; one model per intruder approach (four in total). Parameter count not stated.
4Training
Not stated what the output is graded against (the U-Net approximates the mean of each reverse step); K and the β values (a fixed increasing sequence) not given. Trained on its own samples in rounds; no external data.
5Sampling
Starts from pure Gaussian noise and runs K reverse DDPM steps with the threshold set to 0. Over 1000 failure samples were drawn per scenario. Step count not stated.
6Steering
Conditioning on the robustness threshold, plus retraining on its own outputs: sample, simulate in HighwayEnv, keep the lowest-gap 10% ('elite'), retrain, repeat with a tighter cutoff. No gradient guidance.
Denoises inRaw data
NetworkU-Net
Graded onnot stated
Steeringconditioning
retrain on own samples

How diffusion works here. Here the diffusion model does not draw vehicles at all. It generates a 23-step sequence of errors in what the ego vehicle 'sees' of the other vehicle's position and speed. A U-Net is told the starting state and a target minimum gap, and learns to denoise such error sequences. It trains on its own output: sample errors, run the simulator, keep the 10% that came closest to a crash, retrain, and repeat. At test time it is asked for a gap of zero and returns crash-causing errors. Idea worth remembering: diffusion can learn a system's failure distribution without any crash data.

Used for: Safety validation: finding sensor-error patterns that make an automated vehicle collide with another vehicle at an intersection.

What they found
  • Southern approach, where failures are rarest: the diffusion model's error sequences caused a crash at a rate of 0.2134 (density 0.9002, coverage 0.8045), while the cross-entropy method (CEM) found no failures (Table II).
  • Western approach: diffusion samples covered more of the true (Monte Carlo) failure spread than CEM, with coverage 0.43 vs 0.24 (Table II, Sec. V).

For mobility: An ADAS or automated-vehicle tester could learn which sensor-error patterns make a given intersection approach fail, then target those patterns in simulation or track tests.

Watch out: Tested only on a simplified HighwayEnv intersection with IDM-driven vehicles and a fixed ego policy; in the northern case CEM still had the higher failure rate.

VBD

Huang et al. · IEEE T-ITS 2026 · paper · [D06]
Safety-critical driving scenariosTransformerRaw data
1What is noised (x)
Joint control sequences for up to 64 agents: acceleration and yaw rate over 80 steps of 0.1 s (8 s), shortened to 40 by repeating each action twice. States come from a unicycle model.
2Condition (c)
A query-centric transformer encoder (6 layers, width 256) encodes agent states, 256 map polylines and 16 traffic lights. The denoiser reads these scene tokens through cross-attention; a noise-level embedding is concatenated to the trajectory features.
3Denoiser network
A transformer: self-attention across agents and time (with a causal mask) plus cross-attention to the scene; two decoding blocks, four layers in total. An MLP outputs clean actions. Parameter count not stated.
4Training
Graded against clean data: predicted actions are rolled out and compared with real trajectories by Smooth L1. K = 50 with a new log noise schedule. Co-trained with a behavior predictor on 486,995 Waymo scenarios.
5Sampling
Starts from Gaussian noise. Standard DDPM with 50 steps took 1.48 s per inference on an RTX 4090; DDIM with 5 steps took 0.16 s. In closed loop, 8 s plans are re-made at 1 Hz.
6Steering
Cost guidance on the denoiser's clean guess, 5 gradient steps per denoising step: goal costs from predicted behaviors, collision-avoidance and 'rush' costs, conflict priors, and a pursuer–evader game for adversarial driving.
Denoises inRaw data
NetworkTransformer
Graded onclean data
Steeringconditioning
cost guidance

How diffusion works here. VBD treats the whole scene at once: the accelerations and yaw rates of up to 64 road users over 8 seconds form one array that is noised and denoised together. A transformer denoiser looks across agents and time and attends to the encoded map, traffic lights and agent states. Training grades the rolled-out trajectory against the real one; a noise-predicting version failed in the authors' test. Sampling takes 50 DDPM steps or as few as 5 DDIM steps. Steering adds cost gradients on the denoiser's clean guess: reach a goal, avoid collisions, drive aggressively, or play a pursuit–evasion game against another car. Idea worth remembering: one model trained only on normal driving yields adversarial scenes through guidance alone.

Used for: Reactive multi-agent traffic for closed-loop AV simulation on Waymo data, plus scene editing and safety-critical or adversarial encounters, all without retraining.

What they found
  • Scene editing on Waymo validation scenes (Table II): the per-agent behavior predictor alone gave 5.61±0.27% collisions and 6.19±0.05% off-road, versus 2.47±0.09% and 1.21±0.14% for the joint diffusion model.
  • Adding a collision-avoidance cost as guidance, with no retraining, cut collisions from 2.47±0.09% to 1.11±0.23% (Table III).

For mobility: A test team could edit a recorded intersection, for example make one car run a stop sign, and let the model make the other road users react realistically.

Watch out: Realism on the Waymo benchmark still trails the best autoregressive models, and the safety-critical and adversarial results are shown only as examples, without crash-rate numbers.

2 · Whole scenes and traffic simulation

Generate whole scenes, sometimes the roads too, and keep the traffic realistic as the simulation runs.

Scenario Diffusion

Pronovost et al. · NeurIPS 2023 · paper · [D10]
Whole scenes and traffic simulationU-NetAutoencoder latent
1What is noised (x)
A small latent grid (4 channels) made by a frozen VAE encoder from a 100 m × 100 m bird's-eye image of all agents; it decodes into oriented boxes with paths from −2 s to +2 s at 1-s steps.
2Condition (c)
The map image, encoded to latent size and stacked as extra input channels (concatenation). Agent tokens (position, heading, size, speeds) and a global scene token pass through small MLPs and enter by cross-attention.
3Denoiser network
A conditional U-Net with ResNet blocks at 32, 16 and 8 pixel resolution (64, 128, 256 channels) and 8-head cross-attention to the tokens. Parameter count not stated.
4Training
EDM method in the VAE latent: noise level σ drawn log-normal, and the network's scaled output graded against the clean latent. The VAE is trained first, then frozen. Agent tokens are masked at random.
5Sampling
Starts from noise with σmax = 20 and integrates the reverse ODE to σ = 0 with Euler steps (Fig. 2c shows 100 repeats). Then decodes and keeps boxes above 80% probability, dropping overlaps.
6Steering
Conditioning only: the map plus agent tokens and a global scene token that sets how many extra agents to add. No guidance or cost terms.
Denoises inAutoencoder latent
NetworkU-Net
Graded onclean data
Steeringconditioning

How diffusion works here. Scenario Diffusion draws a whole traffic snapshot: where vehicles are, which way they face, and their 2-second past and future paths. First, a variational autoencoder learns to squeeze a bird's-eye image of the agents into a small latent grid (a compact code). It also learns to decode the grid back into boxes and paths. Then a U-Net learns to denoise that latent, reading the map image and optional tokens that describe key vehicles. Sampling starts from noise, denoises the latent, and decodes boxes above 80% confidence. Idea worth remembering: tokens let you fix one or two key vehicles and let the model fill in realistic traffic around them.

Used for: Generating initial traffic scenes (vehicle boxes plus short paths) on a map, optionally around described key vehicles, to test automated-vehicle planning.

What they found
  • Map-conditioned generation on Argoverse: position and heading MMD² (a distance between generated and real distributions; lower is better) of 0.093 and 0.108, best in Table 1 including TrafficGen, with 0.895 of path points on drivable area, close to real logs.
  • Without the map input, the same model scored 0.142 position MMD² and only 0.411 of path points on drivable area, similar to picking a random log (Table 1).

For mobility: An agency or AV tester could generate plausible test scenes for a new city before many logs exist there, though transfer to very different areas was weaker.

Watch out: Paths cover only 2 s before and after one snapshot and only on-road vehicles are generated; it sets up a scene but does not run closed-loop traffic.

SceneDiffuser

Jiang et al. · NeurIPS 2024 · paper · [D11]
Whole scenes and traffic simulationTransformerRaw data
1What is noised (x)
A scene tensor: up to 128 agents × 91 time steps (1.1 s history + 8 s future at 10 Hz) × features (x, y, z, heading, length, width, height, one-hot type), normalized.
2Condition (c)
Roadgraph and traffic signals compressed into latent tokens by a Perceiver IO encoder (cross-attention). Known cells (local context) are concatenated with the noisy tensor; the fused context enters by adaptive layer norm. Validity mask = attention mask.
3Denoiser network
A spatiotemporal transformer whose blocks alternate self-attention over time and over agents (base model: 4 layers, width 256, 4 heads; small, medium and large sizes tested). Parameter count not stated.
4Training
v-prediction (target mixes noise and clean scene), α-cosine schedule, continuous noise level. Half the time, noise rises along future time steps to prepare amortized rollout. Multi-task inpainting masks; batch 1024, 1.2M steps.
5Sampling
DPM++ sampler with a Heun solver, 16 denoising steps for one-shot scenes and for the rollout warm-up. Amortized rollout then does one denoising step per 0.1-s simulation step (96 vs 1280 network calls for 8 s).
6Steering
Inpainting: history and pre-filled agent features stay fixed. Generalized hard constraints clip the scene at every denoising step (e.g., no overlaps). An LLM can write the constraints; log perturbation partly noises a real scene, then denoises it.

How diffusion works here. SceneDiffuser stores a scene as one table: agents × time steps × features (position, heading, size, type). Every task becomes inpainting: known cells, such as the history, stay fixed and the model fills the rest. A transformer denoiser attends across time and across agents, reads the map and signals, and is trained with v-prediction. For closed-loop simulation, 'amortized diffusion' keeps a future plan whose noise rises further ahead. Each 0.1-s simulation step removes just one noise step, instead of a full 16-step sampling. Hard constraints, such as no overlapping vehicles, are applied by clipping at every denoising step. Idea worth remembering: spread the denoising work over simulation time.

Used for: Waymo sim-agent simulation: generating or editing initial scenes and rolling out all agents in closed loop at 10 Hz for automated-vehicle testing.

What they found
  • Closed loop at 10 Hz on the Waymo sim-agent benchmark, amortized diffusion scored 0.673 composite realism vs 0.492 for full re-sampling at every step (Full AR); open-loop one-shot scored 0.730 (Table 2, M/1 model).
  • For scene generation, a no-collision hard constraint raised the composite realism metric from 0.516 to 0.558, against 0.593 for logged data (Table 1).

For mobility: A simulation team could perturb logged scenes or inject a cut-in vehicle to create many realistic variants of one recorded event for planner testing.

Watch out: It does not beat the best autoregressive sim agents on the benchmark, and it uses the logged validity mask, so vehicles cannot enter or leave beyond the log.

The autoencoder's 8×8 latent grid (RLM) for a 64 m × 64 m bird's-eye scene: 32 channels for lanes and 32 for agents (8×8×64). Lane polylines, signals and agent boxes are decoded from it afterwards.
2Condition (c)
A one-hot city label (Las Vegas, Boston, Pittsburgh or Singapore), fed together with the noise level σ through adaptive layer norm (AdaLN-Zero).
3Denoiser network
A Diffusion Transformer (DiT): self-attention blocks over the latent grid cut into 1×1 patches, with no down- or upsampling. Two sizes: DiT-L (138M parameters) and DiT-XL (487M).
4Training
Two stages: train the autoencoder, then train the DiT (DDPM algorithm) on latents from the frozen encoder. Noise scale σ is drawn from a log-normal distribution; L2 loss against the added noise. Number of steps T: not stated in the paper.
5Sampling
Start from pure noise at the largest σ and refine down to σ = 0; the decoder then outputs lanes and boxes, keeping those with high existence probability. Step count and runtime: not stated in the paper.
6Steering
Inpainting: lane tokens from a real map are held fixed while agent tokens are denoised. Or a known part of the last tile is fixed to grow a long route. Hard traffic: keep the busiest of 8 samples.

How diffusion works here. SLEDGE first trains an autoencoder that squeezes a 64 m × 64 m bird's-eye scene (lanes, signals, cars, pedestrians, obstacles) into an 8×8 grid of numbers. A diffusion transformer is then trained on these grids: noise is added and the network learns to name it, with the city as a label. Sampling starts from noise and cleans a grid; the decoder turns it into lane lines and agent boxes. Fixing some cells (a real map, or the last tile's edge) and denoising the rest adds agents or extends a route to 500 m. Then rules take over: IDM and lane-following move the agents. Idea: diffuse a fixed-size latent, so scenes with any number of objects become an image-like problem.

Used for: Generating road layouts and initial traffic (vehicles, pedestrians, obstacles, signals) to start closed-loop tests of a driving planner.

What they found
  • Generating the latent grid, DiT-L reached 63.99% precision and 61.60% recall (autoencoder features) and lane-graph Fréchet Reach 0.88 (lower is better), ahead of the same DiT on raster images and of the HDMapGen baseline (Table 2).
  • On hard routes with the busiest generated traffic, the nuPlan challenge winner PDM-Closed failed in over 40% of simulations (Table 3).

For mobility: A test team could generate many varied road layouts and traffic densities to stress-test an automated-driving planner on long routes, without storing terabytes of recorded logs.

Watch out: Diffusion only builds the starting scene; agents then move by IDM and simple rules, so the motion is not learned, and lanes are centerlines with assumed constant widths.

SceneDiffuser++

Tan et al. · CVPR 2025 · paper · [D12]
Whole scenes and traffic simulationTransformerRaw data
1What is noised (x)
Two tables: agents × time × features (on/off validity, x, y, z, heading, size, type) and traffic lights × time × features (validity, x, y, z, light state), normalized to (−1, 1); 91 steps at 10 Hz per clip.
2Condition (c)
Roadgraph tokens from SceneDiffuser's context encoder, read by the transformer, plus inpainting masks and known values: the history steps and the AV states produced by a separate planner.
3Denoiser network
Each table is projected by an MLP to a shared width, stacked, passed through SceneDiffuser's axial-attention transformer backbone, then split and projected back. Parameter count not stated.
4Training
v-prediction, α-cosine schedule, one loss. Invalid cells are set to zero, and a loss mask grades only the validity channel there. Trained on 9.1-s Waymo clips; number of noise steps not stated.
5Sampling
From pure noise; each step predicts the clean scene, 'soft-clips' it (values × predicted validity) and renoises to a lower level. Re-sampled every 40 steps (4 s) for a 600-step (60-s) rollout. Step count and sampler not stated.
6Steering
Fill-in only: history and the planner-driven AV stay fixed through inpainting. No cost guidance; soft clipping is a sampler fix for the on/off channel, not steering.

How diffusion works here. SceneDiffuser++ is a traffic world model: given a map and the recent past, it generates what every other road user and traffic light does next. The scene is two tables, agents × time × features and lights × time × features, denoised together by one transformer. Future cells are filled by denoising, like inpainting a picture, using v-prediction training on 9.1-second Waymo clips. The new piece is an on/off 'validity' channel per agent and time step, kept stable by a loss mask and soft clipping. It lets vehicles appear, hide, reappear or leave, so traffic keeps flowing for minutes. Idea worth remembering: one on/off channel turns a fixed cast of vehicles into a living city.

Used for: Trip-level, point A-to-B closed-loop simulation for testing an automated-vehicle planner, on Waymo data with maps enlarged to a 1 km radius.

What they found
  • With an IDM-driven test car over 60 s, SceneDiffuser++ as the world model gave a composite divergence of 0.2878 from logged traffic statistics (lower is better), the lowest of the three world models, ahead of IDM rules and the original SceneDiffuser (Table 1).
  • Collision and off-road realism were worse than with IDM or SceneDiffuser, partly because new vehicles can be spawned onto the planner's route and many are placed in parking lots (Table 1, Sec. 4.2).

For mobility: An agency or AV tester could run long point-to-point simulated trips where vehicles enter, leave and obey signals, to compare trip travel times and safety rates.

Watch out: Realism falls as rollouts get longer (30 s to 300 s, Table 2), and 'realistic' here means matching logged statistics, not that each simulated trip is safe.

Nexus

Zhou et al. · ICCV 2025 · paper · [D14]
Whole scenes and traffic simulationTransformerRaw data
1What is noised (x)
Every agent's state over 21 frames at 2 Hz (4 past, 1 current, 16 future): position (x, y), heading (sin, cos), velocity (vx, vy), length and width. Each agent-frame token gets its own noise level.
2Condition (c)
Lane centerlines, encoded into fixed-length map tokens (Perceiver IO) and read by map cross-attention. Frame time and noise level enter as a 2D rotary position embedding; past states and goals enter as zero-noise tokens.
3Denoiser network
A diffusion transformer built on SimpleDiffusion: map cross-attention, then four temporal and spatial attention blocks (across frames, across agents) with 256-wide features and adaptive layer norm. Parameter count not stated in the paper.
4Training
Each token gets a random noise level in (0, 1]; MSE between the added noise and the predicted noise (Eq. 4). 80K iterations on nuPlan, Waymo and simulated safety-critical scenes (Nexus-Data).
5Sampling
DDIM, 32 steps from Gaussian noise (18 with step skipping). A schedule gives tokens different noise levels: fully denoised frames are popped and new noisy frames pushed in. 206 ms per step per batch.
6Steering
Goals and history are fixed by setting their noise level to zero. Each step, three hand-written corrections, which the paper calls classifier guidance, push overlapping cars apart, smooth accelerations and pull cars onto lanes.
Denoises inRaw data
NetworkTransformer
Graded onnoise
Steeringconditioning
fill-in (inpainting / fixed values)

How diffusion works here. Nexus generates the future motion of all agents in a scene as tokens, one per agent per 0.5 s frame. In training, each token gets its own random noise level, and a transformer learns to predict the noise while reading the map. So the model learns to complete a sequence, guided by whichever tokens are clean. At sampling time, past states and goal points are set to zero noise and steer the rest. Near-future frames are cleaned first and popped out while new noisy frames enter, so the scene can react to a planner's actions. Hand-written rules nudge cars apart and onto lanes at each step. Idea: a per-token noise level works like a soft mask.

Used for: Generating reactive traffic scenes, including cut-ins and collisions, as a closed-loop world for testing planners and as extra training data.

What they found
  • In goal-conditioned generation on nuPlan, Nexus cut displacement error (ADE) by 4.71 compared with SceneDiffuser, an earlier full-sequence diffusion model (Table 1).
  • Giving each token its own noise level (noise masking) lowered goal-conditioned ADE to 3.42, a drop of 4.11 from a Diffusion Policy baseline that uses one shared noise level (Table 3).

For mobility: A safety team could set an attacking car's goal at the test vehicle's future position to create cut-in or crash scenarios that still react to the tested vehicle.

Watch out: Much of the risky training data is simulated adversarial traffic, and some generated crashes are physically wrong (overlapping boxes), so check every scenario before using it.

3 · Predicting and planning motion

Draw several plausible futures, or several candidate plans, instead of one average answer.

MotionDiffuser

Jiang et al. · CVPR 2023 · paper · [D15]
Predicting and planning motionTransformerCompressed (e.g., PCA)
1What is noised (x)
The joint future paths of all modeled agents. Each path of 80 × 2 (x, y) values is compressed by PCA to 10 numbers. A scene is then a table of agents × 10 PCA coefficients.
2Condition (c)
Scene tokens from a Wayformer encoder (road graph, traffic lights, agent histories), one set per agent; each agent's noisy path cross-attends to its own tokens. The noise level σ is Fourier-encoded and concatenated to the input.
3Denoiser network
A set transformer: repeated self-attention among agents, so paths are generated jointly and in any agent order, and cross-attention to the scene tokens. Parameter count not stated in the paper.
4Training
EDM-style: the network outputs the clean path, graded by L2 against the ground truth, with preconditioning scales. Noise levels σ are drawn from a distribution q(σ), with schedule σ(t) = t. Encoder and denoiser trained end-to-end.
5Sampling
A deterministic ODE solved with Heun's 2nd-order method in 32 steps, starting from Gaussian noise at σmax. Many joint samples are clustered into 6 representative futures for the benchmark. Runtime not stated in the paper.
6Steering
Cost guidance: the gradient of a differentiable cost, computed on the denoised estimate D(S; C, σ), is added at each step. Attractor (reach target points) and repeller (keep agents 5 m apart); gradients are clipped for stability.
Denoises inCompressed (e.g., PCA)
NetworkTransformer
Graded onclean data
Steeringconditioning
cost guidance

How diffusion works here. MotionDiffuser generates the futures of all agents in a scene together, as one joint sample. Each path is first compressed with PCA; 3 components already explain 99.7% of the variance, and 10 are kept. In training, noise is added to real Waymo paths. A transformer learns to recover the clean path while reading the map, signals and histories. To predict, it starts from pure noise and denoises in 32 steps; the many joint futures are clustered into six. To steer, a cost is computed on the denoised guess and its gradient is added at each step. Idea: judge the cost on the clean guess, not the noisy sample, so samples obey the goal and stay realistic.

Used for: Multi-agent motion prediction for self-driving cars, and building tailored simulation scenarios with rules or physical limits enforced.

What they found
  • With an attractor pulling each path's end toward a target, the mean end-point error (meanSFDE) was 0.747 and minSADE, a realism proxy, 0.533; fixing paths with an optimizer after sampling met targets but looked unrealistic (Table 2, Fig. 6).
  • A repeller cost between agents cut the overlap rate of joint predictions (agents running into each other) to 0.008, which the authors call an order-of-magnitude drop (Table 2).

For mobility: Build what-if test scenarios, such as a car that must end in a given lane, by writing the goal as a cost and guiding a trained motion model.

Watch out: A guided sample shows what you asked for, not how often it happens in real traffic, so do not read guided scenarios as crash or conflict rates.

DJINN

Niedoba et al. · NeurIPS 2023 · paper · [D16]
Predicting and planning motionTransformerRaw data
1What is noised (x)
The unobserved cells of an agents × time table, each cell a position (x, y) and heading (no heading on Argoverse), scaled to standard deviation 0.5. On INTERACTION, 1 s is observed and 3 s generated.
2Condition (c)
Observed states (past, goals or any chosen cells) plus velocity and size, embedded and concatenated with the noisy states; lane centerlines (10 points each) encoded by an MLP and read by cross-attention.
3Denoiser network
A transformer of 15 layers that alternates self-attention across time (per agent) and across agents (per time step), plus cross-attention to lanes; 256-wide features, 4 heads. Parameter count not stated in the paper.
4Training
EDM formulation: the network outputs the clean unobserved states, graded by L2 (Eq. 6). Noise level drawn from a log-normal distribution. Observation masks are mixed in training (50% past only, 25% goals, others).
5Sampling
Deterministic probability-flow ODE with the Heun 2nd-order sampler, 50 steps from Gaussian noise. For benchmarks, 60 samples per scene are summarized by a 6-component Gaussian mixture.
6Steering
Classifier-free guidance on extra observed states such as goals, with weight λ. Classifier guidance from a small trained cut-in classifier. Scenario editing: noise a hand-edited scene to τ = 0.8, then denoise it.

NetworkTransformer

How diffusion works here. DJINN treats a traffic scene as a table: one row per agent, one column per time step, each cell a position and heading. Some cells are observed (the past, a goal, a whole trajectory) and stay clean; the rest are noised and denoised together. A transformer alternates attention across time and across agents, reads the lane map, and outputs the clean states. Training mixes many observation patterns, so one model can forecast, reach goals or fill gaps. At sampling time, classifier-free guidance sets how tightly samples follow a goal, and a trained classifier pushes scenes toward behaviors such as cut-ins. Idea: choosing which cells are observed turns one model into many tasks.

Used for: Generating joint traffic scenarios for autonomous-vehicle simulation, including goal-directed, cut-in and hand-edited scenes, and joint trajectory forecasting.

What they found
  • Against a jointly trained Scene Transformer on Argoverse validation, DJINN had lower joint scene errors: minSceneADE 0.895 and minSceneFDE 1.758 (Table 2).
  • Cutting the ODE solver to 20 steps cost little accuracy, but 10 steps severely hurt sample quality on INTERACTION (Table 7).

For mobility: A simulation team could hand-edit a recorded intersection scene, or ask for cut-ins, and get realistic joint reactions of the other vehicles for testing.

Watch out: Guided behaviors are only as good as the classifier: the cut-in classifier learned from examples at one merging site, so check that its idea of a cut-in matches yours.

DiffusionDrive

Liao et al. · CVPR 2025 · paper · [D17]
Predicting and planning motionTransformerRaw data
1What is noised (x)
The ego vehicle's plan: 8 (x, y) waypoints over 4 s in the car's own frame. Twenty plans are denoised at once, each starting near one of 20 anchor paths.
2Condition (c)
Scene features from Transfuser's perception (ResNet-34; front cameras plus rasterized LiDAR): bird's-eye-view features read by deformable spatial cross-attention, detected-agent queries read by cross-attention. The step number enters through a timestep modulation layer.
3Denoiser network
A small transformer decoder, not a U-Net: spatial cross-attention, agent cross-attention, feed-forward, timestep modulation, then an MLP giving a confidence score and a path offset. Two cascaded layers; 60M parameters in the whole model.
4Training
Truncated schedule: anchors (K-means clusters of training paths) get only light noise, the first 50 of 1000 steps. Graded against the clean path: L1 loss for the anchor nearest the true path, plus a yes/no score for every anchor.
5Sampling
Start from the 20 lightly noised anchors, take 2 DDIM steps, and keep the plan with the highest confidence score. 45 FPS on an NVIDIA 4090; the planning module takes 7.6 ms.
6Steering
None: it samples. The anchors give a head start, the scene condition shapes the paths, and a learned confidence score picks one plan to drive.
Denoises inRaw data
NetworkTransformer
Graded onclean data
Steeringconditioning
best of many
head start (noised proposal)

How diffusion works here. DiffusionDrive swaps the one-answer planning head of an end-to-end driving model for a diffusion model that proposes several plans. A plain diffusion head on Transfuser needed 20 denoising steps, and different noise samples collapsed onto nearly the same path. The fix: cluster human driving into 20 anchor paths and add only a little noise to them in training (a truncated schedule). The model learns to denoise back to the real path. At run time, noisy anchors are cleaned in 2 steps while the decoder reads sensor features, and a learned score ranks each plan. Idea: start sampling near typical answers, so a few steps still give diverse, realistic options.

Used for: End-to-end autonomous driving: turning camera and LiDAR input directly into the vehicle's own plan in real time.

What they found
  • A plain diffusion head on Transfuser (TransfuserDP) needed 20 denoising steps, ran at 7 FPS, had a mode-diversity score D of only 11%, and raised the driving score PDMS by just 0.6 (Table 2).
  • DiffusionDrive used 2 steps, reached D = 74% and 45 FPS, and scored PDMS 88.1, +4.1 over the regression-head Transfuser (Table 2); PDMS combines collisions, staying on road, time-to-collision, comfort and progress.

For mobility: Seed a generator with typical local maneuvers (anchors clustered from your own driving data) to get fast, diverse candidate plans when testing ADAS features or automated shuttles.

Watch out: NAVSIM is non-reactive: other vehicles replay their logs and do not respond to the plan, so a high PDMS is not proof of safe driving in real traffic.

4 · Sensor data and driving world models

Draw what cameras or LiDAR would record for a given layout, so perception and driving policies can be trained or tested.

GAIA-1

Hu et al. · arXiv 2023 · paper · [D22]

Only the video decoder is diffusion. It denoises short clips of T′ = 7 frames at 288×512 pixels; no latent space is described for it. The world model's discrete tokens (576 per frame) say what each frame should show.

Image tokens (from the tokenizer in training, from the world model at sampling) plus masks marking which frames are given as context. Figure 4 draws tokens joined to each noisy frame; the exact injection layer is not described.

A 2.6-billion-parameter 3D U-Net with separate spatial and temporal attention; temporal layers are switched off for single-image tasks. The 6.5-billion-parameter autoregressive transformer world model is a separate, non-diffusion part.

Graded against the velocity target (v-parameterization) rather than plain noise, with a weighted L1 + L2 loss, a cosine noise schedule and time t′ drawn from U(0,1). Four masked tasks: image, video, autoregressive and interpolation; tokens dropped with p = 0.15.

DDIM, 50 steps, from noise. Decode 7 frames, then extend 5 at a time from 2 overlapping frames, working backwards from the end; then interpolate 6.25 → 12.5 → 25 Hz. Image and video predictions are mixed (w = 0.5).

In the decoder: conditioning on tokens, and fill-in of frames held fixed as context. Content steering (text classifier-free guidance, negative prompts, actions, top-k = 50) happens in the token world model, not the diffusion step.

NetworkU-Net

How diffusion works here. GAIA-1 has two halves, and only the second is diffusion. First, a 6.5-billion-parameter transformer, trained on 4,700 hours of London driving, predicts the next image token. It reads past frames, text, and ego speed and curvature, like a language model writing one word at a time. Those tokens are coarse, so a 2.6-billion-parameter video diffusion decoder turns them into smooth pixels. It starts from noise and denoises 7 frames together in 50 DDIM steps, reading the tokens as its condition. Trained on masked tasks, it can also continue clips and fill in frames between them. Idea to remember: 'what happens' and 'what it looks like' can be split across two models.

Used for: Proposed as a neural simulator that makes realistic and adversarial driving video for training and validating driving systems; the paper shows example videos, not a downstream test.

What they found
  • Denoising frames jointly in one diffusion pass, instead of decoding each frame's tokens on its own, 'greatly improves temporal consistency' of the output video (Section 2.4; stated, no numbers).
  • Commanding left or right steering out of the lane, never seen in the expert training data, still gave geometrically consistent futures; in one, an oncoming car maneuvered to avoid the ego car (Figure 13; examples only).

For mobility: A researcher could replay one real approach to an intersection under different ego maneuvers or weather and see how other road users plausibly react.

Watch out: The evidence is example videos, not measured gains: no test shows the videos improve or validate a driving system, and generation does not yet run in real time.

How diffusion works here. MagicDrive draws the six camera images that match a labeled scene. The labels are a top-down road map, a 3D box per road user, each camera's pose, and a sentence such as 'rain'. Training compresses real nuScenes images into Stable Diffusion's latent space, adds noise, and teaches the network to name that noise given the labels. The pretrained U-Net stays frozen; only the new condition parts learn. Sampling runs 20 UniPC steps from noise, with classifier-free guidance pushing toward the labels. Cross-view attention lets each camera look at its neighbors, so a car spanning two images stays one car. Idea to remember: each condition enters the way its shape suits: the map grid as an added branch, the box list through attention.

Used for: Extra labeled camera images for training top-down (BEV) map segmentation (CVT) and 3D object detection (BEVFusion); the labels are the boxes and map you fed in.

What they found
  • Training the BEV segmentation model CVT with MagicDrive images added (as many as the real ones) raised vehicle mIoU (overlap with the true map) to 40.34 (+4.34) and road mIoU to 79.56 (+5.26) (Table 3).
  • Ablation: feeding boxes only as part of the top-down map image, instead of through their own encoder and cross-attention, left vehicle mIoU on generated scenes at just 5.50 (Table 4, 'w/o Ebox').

For mobility: A researcher could hand-edit box layouts, such as a car turned against traffic or a crowded crossing, and get matching labeled camera images to stress-test a perception model.

Watch out: It cannot create conditions missing from nuScenes: its night images are too bright and requested snow does not appear (Figure 9), so rare weather stays rare.

How diffusion works here. DriveDreamer learns a driving 'world model' from nuScenes video. First, a diffusion model (Auto-DM, built on frozen Stable Diffusion) learns to draw frames that obey a layout. Lane lines and a reference frame are stacked onto the noisy latent, boxes enter through attention, and text sets the weather. Training adds noise to real frame latents and grades the network on naming that noise. Then ActionFormer, a separate transformer, predicts how the layout moves under the ego car's speed and yaw. The diffusion model draws that future, and a small head predicts future actions. Idea to remember: predict the road structure first, then let diffusion paint the pixels.

Used for: Synthetic camera images for training 3D object detectors, plus future video and ego-action prediction checked in an open-loop planning test on nuScenes.

What they found
  • Adding images rendered from 4K training-set layouts raised BEVFusion's 3D detection score to 35.8 mAP (+3.0) (Table 1).
  • With both training stages, the diffusion model reached FID 14.9 and FVD 340.8, image and video realism scores, on nuScenes validation (Table 2, lower is better); the GAN baseline DriveGAN, trained on the same data, scored worse on both.

For mobility: A researcher could render the same intersection layout in rain or at night, or under different ego maneuvers, to grow camera training data for rare conditions.

Watch out: The synthetic images redraw layouts already in nuScenes, so they add new looks, not new rare traffic situations; the FCOS3D detector gained only 0.7 mAP (Table 1).

A 19-channel layout image per view (10 depth, 3 boxes, 3 road map, 3 camera rays) enters through ControlNet, a trainable copy of the U-Net encoder. Text enters by cross-attention. Stage 2 concatenates a first-frame latent with the noisy input.
3Denoiser network
A U-Net initialized from Stable Diffusion 2.1. Its 'decomposed 4D attention' has three parts: within each view, across adjacent cameras, and across frames at the same spot. Parameter count: Not stated in the paper.

Graded against the added noise (Eq. 2). Two weight sets: a multi-view image model (56k steps), then a video model (40k steps) conditioned on a real first frame. Number of noise steps T and schedule: Not stated in the paper.

DDIM sampler, 25 steps, from Gaussian noise. Stage 1 samples the first multi-view frame; stage 2 samples the 8-frame video conditioned on it. Runtime: not given, only called 'relatively high'.

How diffusion works here. Panacea makes labeled six-camera driving videos from a sequence of top-down (BEV) layouts. Each frame's boxes, object depths, road lines and camera rays are drawn as a 19-channel image per camera and fed in through ControlNet; text sets weather and time. Training adds noise to Stable Diffusion latents of real nuScenes clips and teaches the U-Net to name it. Sampling has two stages: first draw one multi-view frame, then draw the 8-frame video conditioned on that frame, 25 DDIM steps each. Its 4D attention links each camera to its neighbors and each frame to the others without the cost of full attention. Idea to remember: split hard video generation into the picture first, then the motion.

Used for: Gen-nuScenes, a synthetic labeled multi-view video set for training video-based 3D detectors (StreamPETR), and turning image-only datasets into video datasets.

What they found
  • Adding Panacea's synthetic videos to the real nuScenes training set lifted StreamPETR's detection score to 49.2 NDS, 2.3 points above training on real data alone (Table 3).
  • Skipping the image-first stage made the videos much worse: FVD rose to 305 (+166) and FID to 36.61 (+19.65) compared with full Panacea (Table 5, lower is better).

For mobility: An agency or test lab could script BEV layouts of a risky work zone or crowded crossing and get matching labeled multi-camera video to test camera-based detection.

Watch out: Synthetic video is not yet as good as real: a detector trained only on Gen-nuScenes reached 77% of real-data performance, and image-to-video lifting cost 2.3 points of mAP.

Latents from the frozen Stable Diffusion autoencoder: six camera images of one moment (multi-view model), or one camera's sequence of frames (temporal model). Training images are 512×512.

A 3D layout image (road, object class, instance ID as colors) passes through a ResNet-like controller; its features are added into U-Net layers. Text and per-object 'local prompts' enter by cross-attention. Video also gets a keyframe and optical-flow token.

Graded against the added noise (Eq. 7), plus a consistency loss from a frozen image-matching network that checks relative camera pose. Multi-view model 50,000 steps, temporal 40,000, fine-tune 10,000. T and schedule: Not stated in the paper.

A cascade using a DDIM sampler (step count not stated). The multi-view model draws frame 1; the temporal model extends each camera; a fine-tune model re-aligns later frames; a sliding window lengthens the video.

How diffusion works here. DrivingDiffusion turns a hand-made 3D layout (road lines plus a box for each road user) into a six-camera driving video. Its denoiser is a Stable Diffusion U-Net working on compressed image latents. The layout is drawn as an image per camera and added into the U-Net through a small controller. Training adds noise to real nuScenes latents and grades the network on naming it, with an extra loss that checks camera geometry between views. Sampling is a cascade: one multi-view frame first, then each camera's video from that keyframe, then cleanup and a sliding window. Idea to remember: a long multi-camera video can be split into simpler diffusion jobs chained together.

Used for: Synthetic labeled multi-view frames to augment training of a BEV 3D detector, focused on rare cases such as close vehicles and unusual headings.

What they found
  • Adding synthetic frames focused on rare cases (close vehicles, unusual headings) raised BEVFusion's detection score (NDS) from 0.412 to 0.434 on nuScenes validation (Table 3).
  • Local prompts (class text attended only inside each object's box) raised the detection score measured on generated images (Object NDS) from 28.1 to 32.6 (Table 4).

For mobility: A safety analyst could edit a recorded layout, for example moving a car into a near-collision, and render matching camera video to probe how a perception stack reacts.

Watch out: Generated frames still fall short of real ones. A pretrained BEVFusion scores object NDS 33.1 on them versus 41.2 on real images (Table 2), so pixels and labels can disagree.

A 16 × 128 latent grid made by an autoencoder from one lidar sweep stored as a 64 × 1024 range image (one row per laser beam, each pixel a distance). 32-beam data use 32 × 1024 images.
2Condition (c)
None, a semantic map (treated as image-to-image translation), camera views (CLIP features of all views, concatenated) or text via the same CLIP space. A condition encoder τθ passes them to the U-Net; token-type conditions use cross-attention.

A U-Net that also reads the timestep. Parameter count not stated. The autoencoder around it (not the denoiser) uses 1 × 4 'curve-wise' convolutions along each beam row with wrap-around padding.
4Training
Two stages. First the autoencoder (L1 reconstruction, 3D point distance, adversarial and vector-quantization losses). Then the U-Net learns to predict the added noise ε (squared error) in the latent. T and noise schedule: not stated in the paper.

Starts from noise in the latent, runs 50 denoising steps in the main results, then the decoder rebuilds the range image. Sampler not stated. 1.603 scans per second on one RTX 3090.

NetworkU-Net

How diffusion works here. LiDM stores each lidar sweep as a range image: a grid where each row is one laser beam and each pixel holds a distance. An autoencoder first learns to squeeze this 64 × 1024 grid into a 16 × 128 latent grid while keeping the beam-shaped curves and 3D point positions. A U-Net is then trained to name the noise added to these latents. Sampling starts from noise, runs 50 denoising steps and decodes the result into a scan. A semantic map, camera views or a text prompt can be fed to the U-Net to steer it. Idea to remember: realism comes mainly from a sensor-aware latent space, not from a bigger denoiser.

Used for: Realistic synthetic lidar sweeps for autonomous-driving perception and simulation, made from cheaper inputs such as semantic labels, camera images or a sentence.

What they found
  • Unconditional 64-beam scenes in 50 steps: 20.4% better FRID and 31.0% better FPVD (realism distances, lower is better) than plain Latent Diffusion with the same number of steps (Table 1).
  • Speed: 1.603 scans/sec vs 0.015 for LiDARGen, a diffusion model working on the full-size range image, about ×107 faster on one RTX 3090 (Fig. 1, Table 3).

For mobility: A researcher with camera-only probe vehicles could create lidar-like scans to test 3D perception, after checking them against real lidar from similar roads.

Watch out: Camera-to-LiDAR only conditions the area the camera sees; the rest is generated freely, and the authors note a generated car 'still struggles with its precise scale in 3D space'.

GAIA-2

Russell et al. · arXiv 2025 · paper · [D23]
Sensor data and driving world modelsTransformerAutoencoder latent
1What is noised (x)
Continuous video-tokenizer latents for up to 5 cameras: a 24-frame 448×960 clip becomes 3×14×30 latents with 64 channels (about 400× smaller). Training windows hold 12,600 tokens; past context latents stay clean.
2Condition (c)
Ego speed and curvature enter through adaptive layer norm, which rescales every layer's features. Camera geometry and timestamps are added to the input. Boxes, road and weather tags, CLIP and scenario embeddings enter by cross-attention.
3Denoiser network
An 8.4-billion-parameter space-time factorized transformer: 22 blocks (width 4096, 32 heads), each with spatial attention over space and cameras, temporal attention, cross-attention and an MLP.
4Training
Flow matching: the input is a straight-line mix τx + (1−τ)ε, graded (L2) against the velocity x − ε, the direction from noise to data. τ comes from a two-peaked distribution: mostly moderate noise (80%), some near-pure noise (20%).
5Sampling
50 denoising steps on a linear-quadratic schedule. It starts from pure noise (from scratch), after clean context (rollouts, sliding window), or from a partly noised real clip (editing). Runtime: not given; real time is 'computationally intensive'.
6Steering
Conditioning by default. Classifier-free guidance (scale 2 to 20) only for rare or out-of-distribution scenes; with agent boxes, only where the boxes are. Masked inpainting inserts agents; partial noising re-renders a real drive in new weather.

How diffusion works here. GAIA-2 is GAIA-1's successor, rebuilt as one latent diffusion model over five cameras and trained on about 25 million 2-second clips from the UK, US and Germany. A video tokenizer shrinks each clip about 400 times, and an 8.4-billion-parameter transformer learns to turn noise into those latents. It is trained with flow matching, a close cousin of diffusion. Instead of naming the noise, it learns the velocity: the straight-line direction from noise to the real latent. Training mixes three jobs: generate from scratch, continue a real clip, and fill a masked region. Idea to remember: one model, three moves, chosen by what you hold fixed.

Used for: Augmenting driving data (re-rendering a real drive in snow or at night) and creating safety-critical test cases: unsafe ego steering, or sudden braking and risky crossings by others.

What they found
  • Design lesson: ego speed and curvature steered the video more accurately through adaptive layer norm than through cross-attention, because an action affects every image token (Section 2.2.1; stated, no numbers).
  • Given real starting frames and a rightward-curvature action, the ego car veered into oncoming traffic and the oncoming car swerved away (Figure 9; examples only, no numbers).

For mobility: A test lab could take one recorded drive and redraw it at night, in rain, or with an added crossing pedestrian to probe a camera-based driving system.

Watch out: Results are mostly example videos and training curves. Nothing is compared with other models or shows that synthetic clips improve a driver, and the data and scenario model are proprietary.

LidarDM

Sensor data and driving world modelsU-NetAutoencoder latent
1What is noised (x)
Only the static 3D scene: a voxel grid whose cells hold a truncated signed distance to the nearest surface and a lidar intensity, compressed by a VAE into a latent. Actors, motion and lidar points are not diffused.
2Condition (c)
The bird's-eye-view map layout (5 classes: lane markings, road lines, edges, crosswalks, driveways), encoded by its own map VAE into a compact latent c. How c enters the U-Net is not stated.
3Denoiser network
A U-Net with 5 ResNet blocks (channels 128, 128, 256, 512, 512). Parameter count not stated. The scene VAE and map VAE are separate ResNet-block networks.
4Training
Predicts the added noise ε (squared error) on VAE latents of pseudo-ground-truth scenes rebuilt from real lidar sequences (NKSR), with moving objects removed. Learning rate 1e-5, cosine decay, 48 h on four A100s. T and schedule: not stated.
5Sampling
Repeated Langevin-style steps, each adding a fresh noise term, denoise the latent until a clean z0; the scene decoder turns it into the 3D scene. Number of steps and runtime: not stated.
6Steering
Classifier-free guidance on the map: each step mixes the map-conditioned and unconditional predictions, (1 + w)·F(z, c) − w·F(z), with guidance scale w (value not stated).

NetworkU-Net
Graded onnoise

How diffusion works here. LidarDM first builds a world, then scans it. From a bird's-eye-view map, a latent diffusion model generates only the static 3D scene: a grid of distances to surfaces plus lidar intensity. It was trained to name the noise added to VAE latents of real scenes rebuilt from lidar sweeps, and classifier-free guidance keeps samples faithful to the map. Cars and pedestrians come from separate 3D generators (GET3D, AvatarClip) and follow replayed Waymo trajectories with an Intelligent Driver Model. A raycaster plus a learned U-Net raydrop model then produces each lidar frame. Idea to remember: diffuse the world once and simulate the sensor physically, so frames stay consistent over time.

Used for: Layout-controlled, time-consistent lidar videos for testing and pre-training 3D detectors and motion planners, and for adding lidar output to traffic simulators such as Waymax.

What they found
  • Frame-to-frame consistency: 7.12% outlier points (more than 0.5 m off) for LidarDM vs 20.56% for a baseline diffusion model that denoises 5 lidar frames at once (Table II).
  • Pre-training a 3D car detector (CenterPoint) on LidarDM frames before real-data training gave 61.3% mAP, higher than training on real data alone (Sec. IV-E).

For mobility: A researcher with lane-level maps of local intersections could generate labeled, time-consistent lidar sequences there to pre-test 3D detectors or planners before costly data collection.

Watch out: Diffusion makes only the static background; actor shapes, motion and intensity come from other models and hand-tuned physics, so their errors are not fixed by the diffusion model.

How diffusion works here. Cosmos-Drive-Dreams turns labeled scenes into many new videos. The road layout and vehicle boxes are drawn into each camera view as an 'HD-map video'. A large video diffusion transformer, already trained on driving footage, denoises video tokens while a side branch reads this map video, so cars and lanes land where the labels say. Only the side branch is trained; the base stays frozen. An LLM rewrites the caption (rainy, foggy, night) to vary appearance, a second model adds the other camera views, and a VLM throws out clips with artifacts. Idea to remember: the labels stay true while the weather changes, so every synthetic clip arrives already annotated.

Used for: Synthetic multi-camera (and lidar) training clips, especially rain, fog and night versions of real scenes, for 3D lane detection, 3D object detection and driving-policy learning.

What they found
  • 3D lane detection on RDS-HQ (2k clips): adding generated clips improved F1 by 10.4% on rainy and 9.4% on foggy test clips over real data only; pixel-level weather effects (Albumentations) helped less (Table 1).
  • Camera 3D vehicle detection with only 1K human-labeled real clips: adding generated clips raised LET-AP by 55.0% relative to real clips alone (Fig. 16, left).

For mobility: An agency could re-render its own labeled corridor recordings under fog, heavy rain or night, conditions it rarely captures, to stress-test camera-based detection before deployment.

Watch out: These are NVIDIA's own 7B models and mostly internal data; the paper omits sampling and training-target details, and quality control rests on a VLM filter, not human review.

Trajectory model: the scene from a single initial frame (road map, vehicle states); how it enters is not stated. Video model: 3D boxes, HD maps, camera settings, multi-view initial frames and a time/weather text prompt.

Not stated in the paper. The trajectory denoiser is reused from CTG and the video denoiser is the published UniMLVG model; neither architecture is described here.

The trajectory model was retrained on the nuScenes training split for 80,000 steps with a one-frame history. No training of the video model is described. Prediction target and T: not stated in the paper.

Trajectories: closed loop, denoise future paths, apply the first few steps, update the scene, repeat. Video: autoregressive 19-frame windows, each starting from the last frame of the previous one. Steps and sampler: not stated.

Cost guidance on trajectories: stage 1 pulls the chosen adversary toward the ego car, with no-collision and on-road costs; stage 2 re-denoises only the ego path with no-collision and on-road costs so it evades. Failed runs are discarded.

How diffusion works here. SafeMVDrive chains two diffusion models. First, a vision-language model looks at the six camera images and picks the vehicle most able to threaten the ego car. A trajectory diffusion model, trained on nuScenes driving, is then steered by cost gradients: in stage one the adversary is pulled into a collision; in stage two the adversary keeps that path while only the ego path is re-denoised to dodge it. The resulting boxes and maps condition a diffusion video generator that renders 9-second multi-view clips. Idea to remember: video generators cannot draw crashes they never saw, so the method asks for a near miss instead.

Used for: Multi-camera near-crash test videos (cut-ins, sudden braking, fast rear approaches) for stress-testing vision-based end-to-end driving planners such as UniAD.

What they found
  • Versus a naive pipeline that renders collision trajectories directly, SafeMVDrive videos made UniAD collide in more samples per scene (scene-level collision rate 3.4 vs. 1.8), and the naive videos had only about half the realism (Table 1).
  • In the user study, SafeMVDrive videos reached 87% of the realism score of videos made from the original, non-critical nuScenes trajectories (Sec. 1).

For mobility: A safety team could turn ordinary logged drives into near-crash camera videos to check whether a vision-based ADAS reacts properly to cut-ins and sudden braking.

Watch out: The dataset is small (41 nine-second scenes from 250 starts), only one planner (UniAD) is tested, and the method needs a fully labeled initial scene, not raw camera video.

Stage 1: one vehicle's future path, a fixed-length list of 2D waypoints (T × 2) in a local frame, sampled in batches of B candidates. Stage 2: six-camera video rendered by the MagicDriveDiT diffusion model (sizes not given).
2Condition (c)
Trajectory model: none, it is unconditional; scene context enters only later through the scorer. Renderer: BEV road maps and 3D bounding boxes of all objects (how they enter is not stated).
3Denoiser network
Not stated for the trajectory model. The renderer is MagicDriveDiT, which the paper groups with DiT (diffusion transformer) video models; its size is not stated.
4Training
Trajectory model trained on nuPlan driving logs (larger than nuScenes) to learn ordinary, human-like paths. Prediction target, T and schedule: not stated. MagicDriveDiT is a published model trained on nuScenes; no retraining is described.

Round 0 denoises a batch from pure noise over all T steps. Then 5 refinement rounds: resample good candidates, add partial noise (level t_trunc), re-denoise. Trajectory sampling took 17.36 s of an 818.62 s scene.

No guidance inside the denoiser. A physics simulator (LQR controller plus kinematic bicycle model) and a score (stay on road, no collision, get close to the ego car) decide which candidates are re-noised and kept; the best one wins.
Denoises inRaw data
NetworkNot stated
Graded onnot stated
