adversary + head start

How diffusion works here. Challenger picks one background car in a real nuScenes scene and makes it drive aggressively. An unconditional diffusion model, trained on nuPlan paths, proposes a batch of ordinary-looking trajectories from noise. Each is tracked by an LQR controller on a bicycle model, then scored for staying on the road, avoiding crashes and getting close to the ego car. The best candidates are resampled, partly re-noised and denoised again for five rounds, a search that keeps the paths human-like. Finally MagicDriveDiT, a diffusion video model, renders the updated boxes and map as six-camera video. Idea to remember: search over cheap abstract trajectories first, then render only the winner.

Used for: Photorealistic multi-camera adversarial videos (cut-ins, tailgating, lane blocking) to stress-test vision-based end-to-end driving models such as UniAD, VAD, SparseDrive and DiffusionDrive.

What they found
  • On Challenger's Adv-nuSc videos, UniAD's average collision rate was 3.95%, a 12.6× increase reported in Table 1; SparseDrive's was 1.026% (8.6×) (Table 1).
  • Ablation: the full pipeline made UniAD fail in 6.17% of generated samples; removing the multi-round refinement or the trajectory scorer gave lower rates (Table 2).

For mobility: A testing agency could take logged scenes from its own corridors and auto-generate aggressive cut-in or tailgating videos to probe camera-based driving systems before road tests.

Watch out: Tests are open-loop on renderer output: the ego car follows its logged path, the renderer cannot draw crashes, and generated video is slightly less consistent than real footage (Table 3).

5 · Traffic data and mobility records

Fill gaps in detector data, forecast with uncertainty, and make trips and OD tables that keep real patterns.

PriSTI

Liu et al. · ICDE 2023 · paper · [D29]
Traffic data and mobility recordsTransformerRaw data
1What is noised (x)
Only the missing cells of a sensors × time table, e.g., 207 METR-LA freeway speed sensors × 24 five-minute steps. Observed cells are never noised.
2Condition (c)
A linear-interpolation fill of the observed data plus the sensor distance graph. A conditional feature module turns them into a prior that sets the attention weights; the interpolation is also concatenated with the noisy values.
3Denoiser network
Four layers of temporal attention, then spatial attention plus a graph message-passing network (Graph WaveNet's graph convolution); 64 channels, 8 heads, gated activations with residual and skip links. Parameter count not stated in the paper.
4Training
Predicts the added noise (L2 loss, Eq. 4). DDPM with a quadratic schedule, β from 0.0001 to 0.2; T = 50 steps for traffic, 100 for air quality. Random points or blocks of real readings are hidden as targets.
5Sampling
DDPM reverse process over all T steps, starting from Gaussian noise in the missing cells (Algorithm 2). 100 samples give a median and a 5–95% band. On METR-LA, 17.9% more inference time than CSDI.
6Steering
None beyond conditioning: the observed readings, their interpolation and the sensor graph shape every step, and observed cells are kept as given. No guidance term.
Denoises inRaw data
NetworkTransformer
Graded onnoise
Steeringconditioning
fill-in (inpainting / fixed values)

How diffusion works here. PriSTI treats gaps in detector data as fill-in-the-blank for a diffusion model. The input is a window of readings from many sensors, such as 207 Los Angeles freeway detectors (METR-LA). A graph says which sensors are close. First, each sensor's gaps get plain linear interpolation, a noise-free first guess. Training hides some real readings and teaches the network to predict the noise added to them. The guess and the graph tell it which times and neighbouring sensors matter. Imputation starts from random noise in the missing cells only and removes it step by step, 100 times over, giving a median and a band. Idea: give the diffusion model a cheap first guess.

Used for: Filling gaps in traffic-speed detector data (random dropouts, 1–4 hour outages) and air-quality station data, including fully failed stations, before forecasting or analysis.

What they found
  • At the highest missing rate tested on METR-LA, with gaps in long blocks, PriSTI's mean absolute error was 4.67%-34.11% lower than BRITS, GRIN and CSDI, an earlier diffusion imputer (Fig. 5).
  • A forecaster (Graph WaveNet) trained on PriSTI-filled Beijing air-quality data reached MAE 29.34, vs 36.97 on the raw gappy data and 30.20 with CSDI filling (Table V).

For mobility: An agency could fill outages in loop-detector or PeMS-style speed data and keep an uncertainty band for every filled value, instead of one silent guess.

Watch out: On the traffic datasets the gaps were injected artificially (random points or blocks), so test it on your own real outage patterns before trusting the filled values.

How diffusion works here. DiffSTG stacks the last 12 and next 12 five-minute flow readings from 170 PeMS detectors into one sensors × time block. In training, noise is added to the whole block, and a network called UGnet learns to name that noise. UGnet sees the noisy block next to a copy whose future half is blanked out, and passes information along the road graph between neighbouring sensors. To forecast, it starts from pure noise, denoises in 40 to 100 steps and keeps the future half. Eight runs give eight possible futures; their spread is the uncertainty band. Idea worth remembering: a forecast is gap filling where the gap is the future.

Used for: Probabilistic traffic-flow forecasting one hour ahead at freeway detectors (PeMS08, 170 sensors); also PM2.5 forecasts at air-quality stations in Beijing and Guangzhou.

What they found
  • On CRPS, a score of how well the whole forecast range fits what happened (lower is better), DiffSTG beat the best other probabilistic method by 14.3% on PEMS08 traffic flow and by 5.6% and 4.3% on the two air-quality sets (Table 2).
  • Generating all 12 future steps in one denoising run made it about 40× faster than TimeGrad, an earlier diffusion forecaster that produces one step at a time (Table 3, timed on the AIR-GZ data).

For mobility: A traffic management center could publish detector forecasts with a likely range and plan ramp metering or incident staffing for the high end, not only the average.

Watch out: Its average forecast is still less accurate than the best deterministic graph models (Table 5); what you gain is the uncertainty band, not a sharper single number.

DiffODGen

Rong, Ding, Liu & Li · arXiv 2023 · paper · [D32]
Traffic data and mobility recordsTransformerRaw data
1What is noised (x)
Stage 1: the N × N yes/no matrix of which census-tract pairs exchange commuters. Stage 2: the N × N commuter counts on those pairs. N = 721 to 1,319 tracts (LODES 2018 commutes).
2Condition (c)
Each tract's census demographics and OpenStreetMap POI counts, embedded (MLPs; GATs in stage 2) and fused by cross-attention into node features and edge features (origin, destination, distance). Node statistics such as degree are added.
3Denoiser network
A graph transformer: tracts are nodes, OD pairs are edges, attention between tracts also uses edge features, and a final layer outputs the N × N matrix. 2 layers (stage 1), 3 layers (stage 2), 64 channels.
4Training
Stage 1 is discrete diffusion (cells randomly flipped between 0 and 1), graded against the clean 0/1 matrix by cross-entropy. Stage 2 is graded against the noise, only on kept pairs. T = 1000, cosine schedule; trained on Cook County.
5Sampling
Stage 1 starts from a uniformly random 0/1 matrix, stage 2 from Gaussian noise on the kept pairs; each runs T = 1000 reverse steps. Pairs without flow are set to zero. Runtime not stated.
6Steering
Conditioning only. The paper calls both models classifier-free conditional diffusion but gives no guidance weight. Stage 1's 0/1 pattern decides where stage 2 generates flows.
Denoises inRaw data
NetworkTransformer
Graded onnoise
Steeringconditioning

How diffusion works here. DiffODGen drafts a commuting OD matrix for a city with no travel survey, using only census and map features of each census tract. It treats the matrix as a network: tracts are nodes and OD pairs are edges. Stage 1 uses discrete diffusion, which randomly flips cells between 0 and 1, to generate which tract pairs have any commuters; this keeps the matrix sparse. Stage 2 uses ordinary Gaussian diffusion to generate flow volumes only on those pairs. Both denoisers are graph transformers that read each tract's features and statistics such as node degree. Idea worth remembering: generate the whole matrix jointly, so city-wide patterns like sparsity and heavy-tailed flows come out right.

Used for: Generating commuting OD matrices for cities without travel surveys, for urban planning, traffic control and simulation.

What they found
  • Trained on Cook County and tested on new cities, flow errors (RMSE/NRMSE) were over 3% lower in New York City and 13% lower in Seattle than the best baseline (Table 2).
  • In New York City, 24.9% of real tract pairs have commuters vs 33.0% in DiffODGen's matrix, while the deep regression baselines came out far too sparse or too dense (Figure 4, Table 3).

For mobility: An MPO or city without a recent household travel survey could draft a commuting OD matrix from census and POI data to seed demand models, then check it against counts.

Watch out: Only home-to-work commutes, trained on one county and tested on two cities; a plain diffusion model on the raw matrix was hardly comparable to a simple gravity model.

DiffTraj

Zhu et al. · NeurIPS 2023 · paper · [D34]
Traffic data and mobility recordsU-NetRaw data
1What is noised (x)
A taxi GPS trip resampled by linear interpolation to a fixed 200 points × 2 (longitude, latitude); trips under 120 points dropped. Trips from Chengdu and Xi'an, November 2016.
2Condition (c)
Trip attributes: numbers (distance, speed, travel time, length) through a wide layer, categories (departure time, start and end regions) through a deep embedding network; added with the step embedding into every residual block.
3Denoiser network
Traj-UNet: a 1-D convolution U-Net (kernel 3; 4 sampling blocks, 2 residual blocks each) with an attention block in the middle and a 128-d sinusoidal step embedding. Parameter count not stated.
4Training
Graded against the noise (mean squared error). T = 500 steps, linear β from 0.0001 to 0.05. Conditional and unconditional versions are trained jointly (attributes zeroed) to allow classifier-free guidance.
5Sampling
Starts from pure Gaussian noise; skip-step (DDIM-style) sampling. About 100 steps matched full 500-step quality and saved 81% of the time; fewer than 100 degraded trips (Fig. 3). Output resized to the wanted length.
6Steering
Classifier-free guidance on the trip attributes: ε = (1+ω)·ε(x | c) − ω·ε(x | ∅), guidance scale 3, presented as a quality–diversity trade-off. Choosing attributes such as start and end regions steers the trips.
Denoises inRaw data
NetworkU-Net
Graded onnoise
Steeringconditioning
classifier-free guidance

How diffusion works here. DiffTraj learns from millions of taxi GPS trips recorded in Chengdu and Xi'an in November 2016, then draws new, synthetic trips. Each trip is resampled to 200 latitude–longitude points, so it becomes a short two-row signal. In training, noise is added to real trips. A 1-D convolution U-Net (Traj-UNet) learns to name that noise, given the step number and trip attributes such as regions, departure time, distance and speed. To generate, it starts from pure noise and removes it in about 100 of the 500 steps, with classifier-free guidance on the attributes. Idea worth remembering: once a trip is a fixed-length signal, image-style diffusion tools carry over.

Used for: Privacy-minded synthetic GPS trips that can stand in for raw traces in analyses such as grid inflow/outflow forecasting.

What they found
  • Flow-prediction models trained on synthetic trips almost matched those trained on real trips: AGCRN inflow MSE 4.33 with real data vs 4.55 with DiffTraj data (Table 2).
  • Trips from other generators were less useful for the same task: inflow MSE 6.78 (GAN), 6.79 (VAE) and 4.62 (Diffwave) vs 4.50 for DiffTraj (Table 6).

For mobility: An agency could share synthetic GPS trips that keep city-wide travel patterns so analysts can build demand and flow models, after first testing the data for privacy leaks.

Watch out: The paper argues privacy because trips are generated from noise but runs no privacy attack such as membership inference, so synthetic here is not proven private.

CoDiffMob

Zhang et al. · WWW 2025 · paper · [D33]
Traffic data and mobility recordsU-NetRaw data
1What is noised (x)
One person's one-day trajectory: 48 time steps × 2 (latitude, longitude), from mobile-network location records in Shanghai (ISP data) and Nanchang (MME data).
2Condition (c)
The step number and the trajectory's starting (home) location; how they enter the U-Net is not stated. Real OD flows and the population map never enter the network, only the starting noise.
3Denoiser network
A 1-D U-Net following DiffTraj: 1-D convolutions on the down- and up-sampling paths and attention after downsampling; hidden size 128, channel multipliers 1, 2, 2, 2. Parameter count not stated.
4Training
Main text: plain random noise at a random level, and the network predicts the noise. Appendix A.2 instead gives an EDM-style loss grading the denoiser against the clean trajectory. Number of steps not stated.
5Sampling
Deterministic DDIM (no added randomness), K steps (K not stated), started from the noise prior instead of pure noise. Runtime not stated.

A noise prior. Rule-based trips that follow real OD flows are run backward through DDIM into noise. Fresh random noise is added, and variance is scaled to hourly moving probability. Table 3 lists guidance scale 3, unexplained.
Denoises inRaw data
NetworkU-Net
Graded onnoise
Steeringconditioning
head start (noised proposal)

How diffusion works here. CoDiffMob generates one-day trajectories of synthetic people, 48 latitude–longitude points each, using a 1-D U-Net denoiser trained on mobile-network records from Shanghai and Nanchang. With DDIM, a sampler with no added randomness, each starting noise maps to exactly one trajectory. The authors found that each move's direction follows the direction in that noise. So they build the starting noise instead of drawing it at random. A rule-based travel model draws rough trips that follow real OD flows; DDIM run backward turns them into noise; fresh random noise is added. Idea worth remembering: you can steer a diffusion model, without retraining it, by choosing where its noise starts.

Used for: Synthetic one-day trajectories that reproduce city OD flows, for planning studies and as extra training data for next-location prediction models (LSTM and Transformer).

What they found
  • City-wide flow match (CPC, where 1 means identical OD flows): 0.6842 vs 0.3992 for DiffTraj, a similar diffusion model started from plain random noise (Table 1, Fig. 3, Shanghai data).
  • Removing the noise prior, so sampling starts from plain random noise, cut CPC to 0.3416 and raised the flow error (MAPE) to 0.8489 on the Shanghai data (Table 2).

For mobility: A city could release synthetic daily trips that reproduce its OD matrix by seeding a diffusion model with trips from a simple travel model it already trusts.

Watch out: It needs real OD flows and a trusted rule-based travel model; better flow match cost some diversity, and privacy was checked only with overlap and membership-inference tests.

PMA-Diffusion

Liu, Jin & Choi · Transportation Research Part C 2026 · paper · [D31]
Traffic data and mobility recordsU-NetRaw data
1What is noised (x)
A time–space speed map of an I-24 MOTION corridor: 200 cells of 100 ft × 200 steps of 1 s (about 3.8 miles × 200 s). Speeds are divided by a fixed v_max; in training only observed cells hold data.
2Condition (c)
In training the denoiser is told the mask (which cells are observed); the paper does not say how the mask enters the U-Net. During sampling no condition enters the network: measurements enter by being pasted in.
3Denoiser network
A U-Net with one input channel, 48 base channels, four resolution levels (channel multipliers 1, 2, 4, 8) and 4-head linear attention in the bottleneck. Parameter count not stated.
4Training
Graded against the injected noise, counted only on observed cells (Huber loss in practice). T = 500, linear β from 10⁻⁴ to 2×10⁻². A 'double mask' hides extra observed cells so always-seen detector rows still get practice.
5Sampling
Starts from pure noise and runs 500 reverse steps, RePaint-style, with occasional small forward re-noising jumps. Each step: denoise, paste observations, apply the physics step. Repeated runs give an ensemble. Runtime not stated.
6Steering
After each step, measured cells are reset (fill-in). Then adaptive anisotropic smoothing (AAS) updates only missing cells: smoothing along free-flow and congested wave slopes, blended by a soft speed gate, plus a small kinematic-wave correction.
Denoises inRaw data
NetworkU-Net
Graded onnoise
Steeringfill-in (inpainting / fixed values)

How diffusion works here. PMA-Diffusion treats traffic state estimation as filling in a time–space speed map of the I-24 corridor (100 ft × 1 s cells). Training sees only gappy maps: noise is added, and a U-Net learns to name the noise only on cells that were measured; a 'double mask' hides extra cells so always-observed detector rows still get practice. To estimate a new map, it starts from noise and runs 500 steps. After each step it pastes the measured speeds back, then smooths the missing cells along free-flow and congested wave directions (adaptive anisotropic smoothing). Idea worth remembering: physics enters at sampling time, so one learned prior serves any sensor layout.

Used for: Highway traffic state estimation: rebuilding full speed maps, including stop-and-go waves, from sparse loop-detector rows and probe-vehicle traces.

What they found
  • With a prior trained on complete maps, 5% of rows observed and no probes, the error on hidden cells (Masked-MSE) was 0.1463 for physics smoothing alone, 0.0172 with diffusion inpainting (RePaint) and 0.0167 with PMA's physics step added (Table 2, Fig. 6).
  • Trained on sparse data only, in that same sparsest case the double-mask prior reached 0.0289 vs 0.0364 for the plain single-mask prior, closing part of the gap to the complete-data prior (Table 2).

For mobility: An agency with loop detectors and a few percent of probe vehicles could rebuild corridor speed maps, including stop-and-go waves, and reuse the same model when detectors change.

Watch out: Ground truth came from I-24 MOTION camera data masked on purpose; real loop and GPS data add bias and time delay that the authors assumed away.

6 · Road damage images

Paint cracks and potholes onto road images you already have, so small agency datasets stretch further.

How diffusion works here. RoadFusion learns what normal pavement looks like and flags the rest as defects. Defect photos are scarce, so the authors take clean road photos, draw a mask where a defect could be, and ask a latent diffusion model (from the earlier DIAG method) to paint a crack or pothole there from a text prompt. The paper gives no diffusion training or sampling details; the generator is used as a ready-made tool. Features of real clean images and of the synthetic defect images pass through two separate adapters, and a small network learns to score each patch as normal or defective. At test time only the real-image path runs. Idea to remember: the generator only supplies the rare class.

Used for: Training a pixel-level pavement defect detector (crack and pothole heat maps) when few labeled defect images exist; the generator is switched off at test time.

What they found
  • EDM Crack (fine cracks, Edmonton roads): IoU (overlap between predicted and true defect pixels) 0.72 vs 0.67 for the best earlier method (Table 1).
  • Crack500: Macro-F1 (a balanced detection score) of 0.91, the highest among the methods compared (Table 1).

For mobility: A city or DOT with many clean pavement photos but few labeled cracks could paint realistic defects onto them to train a crack and pothole mapping model.

Watch out: The paper reports no run without the synthetic defects, so you cannot tell how much the diffusion model itself helps; each dataset has only one or two comparison methods.

What the papers share

Put the 35 cards side by side and the diffusion recipe barely changes. What changes is everything around it.

  1. One training method, two main networks. Sixteen papers denoise with a U-Net, fifteen with a transformer, and four do not say. Scene and trajectory models mostly use transformers that attend across agents and across time (CTG++, VBD, SceneDiffuser, DJINN). Camera and LiDAR models mostly reuse an image U-Net, often Stable Diffusion’s (MagicDrive, DriveDreamer, Panacea). The network follows the shape of the data; diffusion is how it is trained.
  2. Big data gets compressed first. Twelve papers denoise an autoencoder’s latents instead of the raw data, among them nearly every camera and LiDAR generator. MotionDiffuser compresses trajectories with PCA instead. Trajectory and traffic-data models usually denoise the raw numbers, which are small to begin with.
  3. Three ways to grade the network, one idea. Fifteen papers grade the network on the noise, eleven on the clean data, four on a velocity (v-prediction or flow matching), and five do not say. As the Basics handout shows, these carry the same information arranged differently.
  4. Steering is where the transportation problem lives. Twelve papers guide each step with a cost or a classifier, including eight of the nine safety-scenario papers. Ten hold observed values fixed (gap filling, scene completion, editing). Seven use classifier-free guidance on labels or text. Six start from a noised proposal instead of pure noise, and ten keep the best of many samples.
  5. Fewer steps is a recurring fix. Sampling ranges from 2 steps (DiffusionDrive, starting near typical paths) to 500 (PMA-Diffusion). VBD cut 50 DDPM steps to 5 DDIM steps (1.48 s to 0.16 s); SceneDiffuser spreads denoising across the simulation steps.

How a hint reaches the model

Every paper on this page gives its diffusion model some hint about what to generate. In unCLIP (DALL·E 2) the hint is a CLIP image embedding. Here it is a map and past tracks, a layout of boxes, a sentence, a trip’s departure time, or the output of a scene encoder. The hint helps the denoiser head in the right direction at every step. Papers differ in when they have the hint and where it enters the sampling loop.

Two points keep this picture honest.

  • A hint narrows the target; it does not point back to one recorded x. When the model generates, there is no x to recover. The denoiser has learned what data looks like when the hint is true. How close the output lands to one particular x depends on how much the hint pins down. unCLIP’s image embedding pins down a lot, so you get close variations of one image. SLEDGE’s city label pins down little, so you get any road layout typical of that city. A scene encoder’s summary of the map and past tracks fixes the setting but leaves the future open, which is what you want when you need several plausible futures.
  • Conditioning needs the hint in the training data, paired with x. Many transportation goals are too rare to pair: a crash, a near-miss, a failure of the system under test. Others are rules written after the model was trained. That is why so many papers add their hint while generating instead.

Five routes

RouteUse it when the hint is…Retrain?Seen in
Conditionavailable in the training data, paired with each xyesVBD, MotionDiffuser, MagicDrive, DiffTraj
Guidea rule you can write as a cost (distance, time to collision, staying on the road), or a score learned from labelsno, or only a small scorerCTG, SAFE-SIM, VBD, CCDiff; DiffScene, AdvDiffuser, DJINN
Fill inpart of x itself, observednoPriSTI, PMA-Diffusion, SceneDiffuser, SLEDGE
Head starta rough draft of xnoDiffusionDrive, DJINN, GAIA-2, SAFE-SIM
Selecta verdict you can only check on finished samples, often from a simulatorno; or retrain on the best samplesLangTraj, Challenger, Wang et al.

The same hint can travel by different routes. DiffSTG feeds past detector readings to the network as a condition. PMA-Diffusion never shows the readings to the network: it pastes them back after each step and then applies a traffic-physics smoothing step. Conditioning learns to use the hint well, but only for the patterns of missing data it saw in training. Fill-in works for any pattern of gaps without retraining.

Conditioning: what the hint is

  • A scene summary from a scene encoder: the map, past tracks and signals. The usual choice for trajectories (CTG, VBD, MotionDiffuser, SceneDiffuser).
  • A layout drawn as an image: a top-down map, 3D boxes, or an HD map rendered into the camera view. The usual choice for camera and LiDAR data (MagicDrive, Panacea, Cosmos-Drive-Dreams).
  • Text: weather and time of day (MagicDrive, Panacea), a scenario sentence (LangTraj), a pavement-defect description (RoadFusion).
  • Labels and attributes: the city (SLEDGE), trip distance and departure time (DiffTraj), census and point-of-interest counts (DiffODGen). Even danger itself: Wang et al. condition on the wanted minimum gap between two vehicles, then ask for a gap of 0.
  • Another model’s embedding, the closest cousin of unCLIP. LiDM conditions LiDAR on CLIP features of the camera images, then swaps in CLIP text features to get text-to-LiDAR with no extra training.
  • Ego actions: speed and curvature (GAIA-2), or a turn sequence (DriveDreamer).
  • Who affects whom: CCDiff’s causal graph limits which vehicles each vehicle can attend to.

Conditioning: how the hint gets in

Match the route into the network to the shape of the hint.

  • Lined up cell by cell with x (a history block, an interpolated speed map, a map raster): stack it with the noisy input. DiffSTG, PriSTI, Scenario Diffusion.
  • A dense layout image for a big pretrained image model: a side branch (ControlNet-style) whose features are added into the network. MagicDrive, Panacea, Cosmos-Drive-Dreams.
  • A set of things (lanes, vehicles, boxes, words): cross-attention, so each part of x looks up the parts of the hint it needs. VBD, MotionDiffuser, LangTraj. This is door 2 in the unCLIP handout.
  • One global setting that should affect everything: scale-and-shift in every layer (adaptive normalization). SLEDGE’s city, DiffTraj’s trip attributes, GAIA-2’s ego actions. This is door 1 in the unCLIP handout. GAIA-2 reports that ego speed and curvature steered the video more accurately this way than through cross-attention, because an action affects every part of the image.
  • A rule about interactions: an attention mask. CCDiff.

Classifier-free guidance is a dial on top of conditioning. It compares the network’s guess with and without the hint and pushes further in the direction the hint points. The papers that report a setting keep it low (MagicDrive 2, DiffTraj 3, CCDiff below 2); GAIA-2 turns it up (2 to 20) only for rare scenes. Higher settings follow the hint more closely and lose variety, which is why LangTraj keeps its weights moderate.

Going deeper (optional): the routes in the notation of the Basics handout

The denoiser g(zt, w, t, c) guesses the noise in zt; the clean guess is x̂ = (zt − √(1 − αt)·g) / √αt.

  • Condition: train g with c as an extra input. Nothing changes in sampling except that c is read at every step.
  • Classifier-free guidance: g = gwithout + (1 + λ)(gwith − gwithout). λ = 0 is plain conditioning; tools report s = 1 + λ.
  • Guide with a cost J: gguided = g + λ·√(1 − αt)·∇J(x̂), with the gradient taken with respect to zt. This moves the clean guess downhill on J; λ sets how hard.
  • Fill in: after each step, overwrite the observed cells with the observed values noised to the current level, √αt·xobs + √(1 − αt)·ε.
  • Head start: begin at an earlier step τ from √ατ·xdraft + √(1 − ατ)·ε instead of pure noise at step T. Less noise keeps more of the draft.

Sources: Ho & Salimans (2021) for classifier-free guidance; Dhariwal & Nichol (2021) for guidance by a gradient; Lugmayr et al. (2022, RePaint) for fill-in; Meng et al. (2022, SDEdit) for the head start.

Which route for which job

A scenario described in wordsno such pairsa language model writes the cost; then guideCTG++
Camera or LiDAR data for a layoutlayout–image pairsside branch or stacking for the layout; text for the weatherMagicDrive, Panacea, Cosmos-Drive-Dreams

The classical baseline to beat: a scripted scenario with a parameter sweep (SUMO, CARLA, OpenSCENARIO) for safety tests; a game-engine render for camera data; interpolation, kriging or the adaptive smoothing method for detector gaps; a gravity model for OD flows; a rule-based or optimization planner for ego plans.

The strongest papers combine routes: condition for realism, guide toward the goal, select at the end (CTG, SAFE-SIM, LangTraj).

The one question to ask: where does your hint come from? From the training pairs: condition. From a rule: guide. From observed values: fill in. From a draft: give it a head start. Only from a test result: select.

Where it breaks

  • Push too hard and realism goes. Every route but conditioning pulls the sample away from what the training data looked like. CCDiff guides only the few vehicles that matter; that cut the share of vehicles whose realism push and guidance push point in opposite directions from about 9.1% (CTG) to 4.8%.
  • A cost rewards what you wrote, not what you meant. A collision cost will happily produce a crash no vehicle could drive. CTG re-rolls positions from actions at every step, and CCDiff passes actions through vehicle dynamics, so guided paths stay drivable.
  • A condition must be available when you generate. A model conditioned on HD maps cannot run where no HD map exists.
  • A hint that pins down too much returns copies. For synthetic trips (privacy) and test scenarios (coverage), check that samples are not near-copies of training records.
  • Selection is costly for rare goals. Keeping the best of 64 is cheap; finding a one-in-a-million failure by sampling alone is not.

Fit card — steering a diffusion model with a hint

Idea in one sentence
A hint about the wanted output enters the sampling loop at one of five places: the network’s input, the clean guess, the starting point, or the finished samples.
Why it works
Every step makes a guess of the clean data. That guess can be informed, pushed, overwritten or seeded before the next step, and the denoiser keeps the result looking like real data.
Fits these tasks
Safety scenarios, sensor data for a layout, trips and OD flows, several possible futures, detector gap filling (generation · prediction).
Needs this data
Recorded x (trajectories, sensor data, detector speeds) plus, by route: hint–x pairs, a cost or labeled scorer, the observed values, a draft, or a simulator.
Breaks when
The push leaves the training data, the hint is missing when you generate, or the cost rewards a physically impossible result.
Keep the classical method when
You only need parameter variations of a scenario you can already script, one fast best estimate of a gap, or results a reviewer can trace rule by rule.

Not on this page: Kalluri et al. (CVPR 2024 Workshops), the disaster-image paper in the reading library, uses no diffusion. It chose MUSE, a masked-token model, over diffusion for easy masked editing. Not every generative paper is a diffusion paper; check before you file it.

Check yourself

1. One paper denoises vehicle paths with a transformer; another denoises camera latents with a U-Net. What is the same about how they are trained, and what differs?

The same: both add noise at a random step and grade the network on recovering the noise, the clean data or a velocity, and both sample by removing noise over many steps. What differs: what is noised (paths or latents), what the network reads (a map and past tracks, or boxes and text), and the network itself. That is why the cards keep the six questions separate.

2. You want left-turn near-misses at a Florida intersection, generated from drone trajectories. Which cards do you read first, and what must you add?

CTG, SAFE-SIM and VBD for steering a model of normal traffic with a cost; SceneDiffuser for holding the recorded turner fixed while the rest is generated. Add the checks from the handout: physics, set-ups inside the recorded range, and how each conflict arises. And remember that a share of steered conflicts is not a crash rate.

3. A detector-gap paper reports better imputation than its baselines. What do you ask before using it on your district’s detectors?

What the baseline is (simple interpolation, kriging, or the adaptive smoothing method); whether the test hides whole sensors and long outages, not just random cells; and how the method does on the ugly cases, such as a queue forming inside the gap. PMA-Diffusion is a good model for adding traffic physics to the sampling loop.

4. Your drone video of one signalized intersection holds thousands of left turns but only about a dozen near-misses. You want hundreds of near-miss scenarios to test a turn-assist system. Which route carries the hint “near-miss”?

Too few near-misses to condition on them directly. Train on all turns, condition on the map and past tracks for realism, and guide the turning vehicle with a time-to-collision cost (as SAFE-SIM and CCDiff do), keeping the best of many. A second option follows Wang et al.: label every recorded turn with its smallest gap, which gives thousands of pairs, condition on the gap, and ask for small gaps. Either way, check that the paths are drivable.

5. Your imputation model conditions on the observed cells and was trained on random five-minute dropouts. Next year whole stations go dark for construction. What may go wrong, and which route avoids retraining?

A conditioned model learned to use the gap patterns it saw; whole-station outages are a new pattern, and it may fill them badly. Fill-in pastes whatever is observed after each step and works for any pattern without retraining, as PMA-Diffusion does. Test either model by hiding whole stations before trusting it.

  • Diffusion Models: The Basics (course handout and Module 4.8): the recipe on this page, built step by step on I-405 detector data.
  • Reading unCLIP (DALL·E 2): From a CLIP Embedding Back to an Image (course handout): a hint that is an image embedding, entering through the two doors described above.
  • Diffusion in the Literature: From Image Generators to Safety Scenarios (course handout): the image papers these models borrow from, and a worked example that steers a scenario model toward intersection conflicts.
  • Reading library: generative models in transportation (Module 4, closing page): VAE, GAN, token and diffusion papers side by side.
  • Peng et al. (2024), Diffusion models for intelligent transportation systems: a survey, arXiv: a broader map of the field.
